deduplication_rule: Canonical URL; locators, limitations, notes and local provenance are unioned.

sources.title: Proto-Cuneiform Account-Books and Journals
sources.author: Robert K. Englund
sources.authority: Leading specialist synthesis grounded in the archaic tablet corpus and CDLI work.
locators: pp. 24–27 (PDF pp. 2–5), especially chronology figure and discussion of Uruk IV/III corpus
limitations: Chronological ranges and corpus counts reflect the state of publication in 2004; some causal interpretation belongs to WS02.
Older chronology; causal interpretation remains debated.
Earliest corpus only.
notes: Supports ca. 3300 BCE emergence, relative Uruk IV→III sequence, overwhelmingly administrative earliest corpus, and caution around token continuity.
Selected for this workstream's bounded question.

sources.title: Uruk and I
sources.author: Hans J. Nissen
sources.authority: CDLI Journal article by a senior Uruk specialist auditing excavation records and chronology.
limitations: Author explicitly foregrounds failures in legacy excavation documentation; exact absolute dates remain model-dependent.
notes: Uruk IVa is the most probable archaeological placement of the oldest script, slightly earlier cannot be excluded; find context is often insufficient and unreliable.

sources.title: Writing in Early Mesopotamia: Beyond the Meme
sources.author: Massimo Maiocchi
sources.authority: Assyriological synthesis focused on early Mesopotamian writing, semiotics and material systems.
locators: pp. 410–412 (PDF pp. 15–17), especially discussion of glottographic/semasiographic boundary
limitations: The chapter advocates a fluid continuum; terminology is analytical rather than a universally accepted threshold definition.
Framework-oriented rather than a new excavation report.
notes: Useful counterweight to a binary true-writing/proto-writing distinction and to a linear token→tablet story.
Selected for this workstream's bounded question.

sources.title: The Origins of Writing
sources.author: Ira Spar
sources.authority: Metropolitan Museum of Art Heilbrunn Timeline essay by a cuneiform specialist.
limitations: Introductory synthesis and now older; statements about possible mid-fourth-millennium Syrian/Turkish systems are provisional.
Introductory; dates rounded.
Broad chronological compression.
notes: States that Sumerian identification of Uruk tablets is popular but not universal; phonetic use is sparse before 3000 and consistently apparent much later.
Selected for this workstream's bounded question.

sources.title: Visible Language: Inventions of Writing in the Ancient Middle East and Beyond
sources.author: Christopher Woods (ed.)
sources.authority: University of Chicago Oriental Institute catalogue curated by a Sumerologist.
locators: comparative chronology and essays on earliest Mesopotamian and Egyptian writing; catalogue overview
limitations: Catalogue compresses specialist disagreements for comparative presentation; use for comparison scope, not exact Uruk stratigraphy.
Comparative overview; some pathways remain hypothetical.
Catalogue compresses disagreements.
notes: Treats Mesopotamia and Egypt as roughly contemporary independent inventions; supports avoiding an unqualified unique 'world first' claim.
Selected for this workstream's bounded question.

sources.title: Visible Language exhibition overview
sources.author: Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures, University of Chicago
sources.authority: Official ISAC summary of the Woods-curated exhibition.
limitations: Public-facing overview rather than full argument; dates are rounded.
notes: Places Mesopotamian tablets around 3200 BCE and early Egyptian tags around 3320 BCE, illustrating why 'first' depends on definition and dating.

sources.title: The State of Decipherment of Proto-Elamite
sources.author: Robert K. Englund
sources.authority: Corpus-based comparison by a leading proto-cuneiform and proto-Elamite specialist.
limitations: Proto-Elamite comparison is secondary to WS01 and does not establish the spoken language of Uruk scribes.
notes: Supports relative order Uruk IV before Uruk III and contemporaneity/contact with proto-Elamite; shows attribution is regional and transmissional, not a simple ethnic label.

sources.title: The Origins of Writing
sources.author: Metropolitan Museum of Art, object and corpus context
sources.authority: Major museum collection context linked to excavated and collected early tablets.
locators: object description: earliest tablets around 3300 BCE; two early phases
limitations: Single object is illustrative, not representative; provenance and dating of market-derived tablets can be weaker than excavated material.
notes: Material anchor for the approximate 3300 BCE date and phase distinction.

sources.title: Reconsidering ‘Tokens’

sources.title: A Quantitative Analysis of Proto-Cuneiform Sign Use in Archaic Tribute
sources.author: Logan Born and Kathryn Erin Kelley, 2021
locators: §§1–3; corpus definition, sign-frequency and genre limits
limitations: Sign-frequency patterns do not by themselves establish sign meanings or causal direction.
Readability, sign variants, genre assignment and corpus growth constrain quantitative conclusions.
notes: Used to test how far administrative subgenres can be distinguished from the preserved corpus.
Used to separate observed sign distribution from reconstructed linguistic value.

sources.title: MSVO 3, 79 artifact entry (P005390)
sources.author: Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative; transliterations by Robert K. Englund, Jacob L. Dahl and CDLI
sources.type: primary artifact record and corpus transliteration
sources.authority: CDLI object-level record linked to the Metropolitan Museum of Art
locators: Text: obverse columns 1–2 and reverse columns 1–2
Edition references: MSVO 3 no. 79; Frühe Schrift no. 4.79; CTMMA IV no. 180
limitations: CDLI labels Uruk provenience uncertain and dates the tablet to Uruk III ca. 3200–3000 BCE; the Met uses Jemdet Nasr ca. 3100–2900 BCE. Language is undetermined and the document lacks verbs, limiting transaction-level interpretation.
notes: Selected administrative object. Contemporary ancient tablet, not a later copy; use as an early economic-classification case, not a transparent voice.

sources.title: Cuneiform tablet: administrative account concerning the distribution of barley and emmer
sources.author: Metropolitan Museum of Art
limitations: The museum gives 'probably from Uruk' and a broad interpretive description; acquisition rather than excavation context means exact provenience is uncertain.
notes: Rights anchor for the selected administrative object: Met object images are marked Public Domain; credit the museum and object number.

sources.title: Cuneiform tablet: private letter
sources.author: Metropolitan Museum of Art
sources.type: primary artifact record with scholarly overview
locators: Overview: Marduk-mushallim's report on non-implementation of a royal security order
Artwork details: Old Babylonian, ca. 1632 BCE, probably Sippar-Yahrurum
limitations: Purchased in 1886; exact archaeological context is unavailable and geography is qualified as probable. The letter is unusual, so it cannot represent ordinary correspondence.
notes: Selected epistolary object. Treat as an ancient documentary letter, not an Old Babylonian school copy. Met object images are marked Public Domain; modern translation wording is not cleared for direct quotation.

sources.title: N 6052 (+) UM 29-16-393 artifact entry (P228744)
sources.author: Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative / Digital Corpus of Cuneiform Lexical Texts
sources.type: primary artifact record, transliteration and composite witness
locators: CDLI P228744; museum nos. N 6052 (+) UM 29-16-393
Witness to CDLI Lexical 000001 / composite Q000001
limitations: Fragmented Old Babylonian school tablet; obverse is not preserved and findspot/stratigraphic fields are blank. It represents formal lexical training at Nippur, not general literacy.
notes: Selected knowledge/training object. Excavated at Nippur, ca. 1900–1600 BCE. CDLI provides transliteration; the photograph is marked © Penn Museum and requires a separate image-use check.

sources.title: Letter from Puzur-Shulgi to Ibbi-Suen about Ishbi-Erra's claim on Isin (ETCSL 3.1.19)
sources.author: Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature, University of Oxford
sources.authority: Curated Sumerian literary corpus with manuscript list and edition bibliography
locators: Cuneiform witnesses include 3N-T311 = IM 58418 and IM 13347; full witness list in bibliography
limitations: The online text is a modern composite reconstructed from multiple Old Babylonian school manuscripts. It is not a surviving contemporary Ur III letter or a single speaker's unmediated voice.
notes: Selected literary-memory text. The narrated setting belongs to the end of Ur III, while the surviving manuscripts are later Old Babylonian copies.
